reply: Fluorescence alone cannot be used to report glucose concentration and viable biomass without first establishing a suitable fluorescent target or marker; the literature notes that fluorimetry requires such a target and is mainly used for endogenous fluorophores like NADH, not for glucose directly. You should first explore whether any intrinsic or added fluorophore can serve as a proxy, and in parallel consider Raman or NIR as alternative or complementary approaches.

risks: Fluorescence may be dominated by background autofluorescence, obscuring weak signals.
Raman signal is intrinsically weak and may require higher laser power or longer integration.
NIR may lack sensitivity for low‑level glucose changes without chemometric calibration.
The proposed signal may follow a related quantity rather than viable biomass.

steps: Collect broth samples across the fermentation time course.
Measure with the existing fluorescence spectrometer; record excitation/emission spectra.
Identify any intrinsic fluorophores (e.g., NADH) that correlate with glucose or biomass using chemometrics.
If a suitable fluorophore is found, build a calibration model against reference glucose (e.g., HPLC) and viable cell count (e.g., CFU).
In parallel, acquire Raman and NIR spectra on the same samples; develop independent calibration models.
Validate each model on held‑out samples (different batches/days).
Then measure in-line or in a pilot set-up against the reference method.
feasibility.decisionBasis: Compare model performance (RMSEP, bias) against agreed acceptance criteria; select the simplest method that meets them. Agree two things separately with the customer before the test: the model accuracy required against the reference method, and the alarm or action threshold applied to the measured value.
